newsitem.title: USA: COMEX copper lower early on light volumes.
newsitem.headline: COMEX copper lower early on light volumes.

text.p: COMEX copper futures were weaker, as expected, after the first hour Thursday, following builds in both LME and COMEX warehouse stocks overnight, but volumes were very light, traders said.
LME copper stocks rose a further 2,000 tonnes Thursday to 145,750 tonnes, while COMEX stocks slipped fell another 1,365 short tons Wednesday to 49,520 short tons.
Activity was slowed by May Day holidays in much of continental Europe and the start of the Golden Week holidays in Japan, traders said.
COMEX July copper was down 1.35 cents at 110.00 cents a pound, after trading a 111.75-108.60 cent early range.

The May/July spread eased further to 0.90 cent from 1.15 cent Wednesday, while the LME cash-to-three month spread was little changed around $68.00 a tonne, after both spreads eased sharply in the past week as prompt market tightness dissipated.
Daily momentum oscillators in July copper suggested the late April rally had begun to wane, analysts said, after nearby COMEX copper saw an eight month high around 119.60 cents in late March.
The July/September spread remained firm though, edging up to 3.50 cents early Thursday.
Potential supply disruptions were being watched also, traders said, after a second strike by workers at Chilean copper mines Wednesday .
Workers at Quebrada Blanca, which produces 75,000 tonnes of cathode a year, went on strike Wednesday after negotiations failed, local union president Nelson Fuentes said.
A small group of workers at the huge Escondida mine, also in Chile, have been on strike for over a week and a half.

On the demand side, the chairman of ASARCO, the world's fourth largest non-state-owned copper company, said Wednesday that the copper market would end 1997 and 1998 with supply/demand deficits of 53,000 short tons and 149,000 short tons respectively.
Western world copper inventories were down to 2.6 weeks, with a further 1.5 weeks in transit, he said.
He blamed poor data by agencies, such as the American Bureau of Metal Statistics, for earlier forecasts by many analysts suggesting the copper market would see supply surpluses this year.
